short: The Admiralty committee that built Britain's first tanks while the War Office looked away.
full:
Winston Churchill, as First Lord of the Admiralty, formed the Landships Committee in February 1915 after the War Office had let proposals for armoured trench-crossing machines lapse. Its chairman was Eustace Tennyson d'Eyncourt, Director of Naval Construction; its members included Flight Commander Thomas Hetherington of the Royal Naval Air Service and the heavy traction engineer R. E. B. Crompton. That the navy paid for a land weapon left its mark on the vocabulary: tanks have hulls and sponsons because warships do.

The committee spent months on schemes for enormous wheeled machines before turning to caterpillar tracks and commissioning William Foster and Co. of Lincoln to build what became Little Willie, and then Mother. Secrecy produced the cover story that the hulls were water carriers for Mesopotamia, and in December 1915 the codename tank was adopted and never shaken off. Churchill left the Admiralty in May 1915, and as the army came round the work passed to the Ministry of Munitions, the committee being reconstituted as the Tank Supply Committee in 1916.
